title: Stem Cell Therapy (Awareness Level)
desc: Understand in plain words what stem cells are, what approved treatments exist, how to spot unproven clinics, and the ethics involved. Awareness only.
outcomes: Explain what stem cells are and the main types.
Use a checklist to judge a clinic or advert.
Separate approved uses from experimental claims.
Weigh hope against evidence and cost.
Draft a short guide for patients and families.
task: Produce a one-page safe-choice guide on stem cell treatments with a clinic checklist and a glossary.
condition: A computer, public information, two peers and a mentor. No medical advice is given and no patient records are used.
standard: Facts are sourced and dated; approved and experimental uses are kept apart; no promise of cure appears; the guide tells readers to ask a qualified specialist; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Patients, carers, teachers, health writers and trainee lab staff.
modules: What stem cells are
Understand
Stem cells can make copies of themselves and become other cell types.
Types: embryonic, adult (tissue) and induced stem cells.
Each type has different uses and limits.
Most bodies already use stem cells every day, for example in blood and skin.
Blood stem cells in bone marrow keep making new blood cells through life.
Draw a simple picture of one stem cell becoming two kinds.
Picture is accurate.
Approved uses
Understand
Some treatments are established.
Blood stem cell transplants for certain blood cancers and disorders are long established.
Skin and eye surface grafts exist for some conditions.
Approval means tested trials and regulators agreed.
A hospital uses a donor transplant for a specific leukaemia after matching tests.
List three approved uses with their source.
Sources are public regulators or hospitals.
Trials and evidence
Analyse
Research moves in stages.
Lab studies, then small human trials, then larger trials, then approval.
Case stories are not proof.
Look for peer review, trial registries and large samples.
A clinic cites patient stories only; the learner finds no registered trial.
Check one claim against a trial registry.
Finding is written with date.
Unproven clinics
Evaluate
Some clinics sell hope without proof.
Red flags: cures many diseases, pay up front, no trial, no follow-up, pressure to decide fast.
Risks: infection, tumours, wasted money, delay of real care.
Ask: Is this approved or in a registered trial?
A family declines an expensive injection after the clinic cannot name any trial.
Score two adverts with the red-flag list.
Each red flag is cited.
Ethics and sources
Evaluate
Questions of consent and respect.
Donors must give informed, free consent.
Debates exist about embryo use; different cultures and faiths hold different views.
Cord blood banking is a personal choice, with limited common uses.
A parents' guide explains cord blood choices without pressure.
Write a balanced paragraph on one ethical question.
Both views are stated fairly.
Talking with specialists
Apply
Come prepared.
Questions: purpose, approval status, risks, cost, alternatives, follow-up.
Take a family member and notes.
A second opinion is normal.
A patient brings a one-page question list to the haematologist.
Make a question list.
Eight clear questions.
Cost, travel and safety
Evaluate
Medical travel adds risks.
Check licence and insurance; plan follow-up care at home.
Count the full cost, not only the fee.
Keep records of every treatment.
A traveller adds flights, hotel and follow-up to the price and decides against it.
Cost a hypothetical trip.
Total includes all items with currency.
Write the guide
Create
Make it useful.
One page, plain words, large print.
Include the checklist and local regulator contacts.
Test with two readers.
Readers say they would ask "is it in a registered trial?" first.
Finish and test.
Readers can repeat three red flags.
quiz: Blood stem cell transplant for some blood disorders.
Cures many diseases; pay up front or fast pressure.
Is it approved or in a registered trial?
Infection, tumours, wasted money or delayed care.
Donors must freely agree with full information.
What cost parts does travel add?
rubric: Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
Checked, dated and explained to others
